title: cdp
text:
Some web work cannot be done with downloads alone. A page may need a login, a click on a button, or a form filled in before it shows anything useful. This module drives a real Chrome through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), the interface Chrome’s own developer tools use, by way of fastcdp.
It uses one long-lived Chrome, separate from the one you browse with. It listens for remote control on port 9223 and keeps its own profile, by default in ~/.cache/fastcdp/cdp-chrome, so anything you log in to there stays logged in across restarts. cdp_connect attaches to that Chrome and starts it first if it is not running; cdp_setup only starts it. cdp_ws returns its websocket address, which scrapling’s browser fetchers accept as cdp_url, and cdp_app opens a URL in it as an app window with no tabs or address bar. debug_ready tells you whether that Chrome is up without starting it: it asks the DevTools endpoint for /json/version, because Chrome opens the port a moment before it can answer there.
The functions here are async, so call them with await, or wrap them in syncy from synchronous code as the examples do. Most of them are methods added to fastcdp’s CDP connection and Page classes. On a page, snapshot gives an agent a short text map of the controls it can use, fill_form and act operate those controls by their visible labels, calls records the network requests the page makes, and md returns the live page as markdown.

text:
Managing the debug Chrome
Chrome’s DevTools endpoint can be inspected with plain HTTP. /json/version describes the browser and /json/list lists its open tabs. The first cell below lists them. The second closes a tab, quits the browser, and starts it again in a visible window with cdp_setup(headless=False), which is how you log in to a site by hand. The cookies are saved in the profile, so they survive later restarts.

# LIST — is a debug Chrome up, and what's open in it?
import httpx
port = 9223
print('running on 9223?', _debug_running(port))
ver = httpx.get(f'http://127.0.0.1:{port}/json/version').json()
print('browser:', ver['Browser'], '| ws:', ver['webSocketDebuggerUrl'])
for t in httpx.get(f'http://127.0.0.1:{port}/json/list').json():   # open tabs/pages
    print(' ', t['type'], '|', t['title'][:40], '|', t['url'][:50])
print('live debug ports:', [p for p in (9222, 9223, 9224) if _debug_running(p)])

# CLOSE a single tab, QUIT the whole browser, then RELAUNCH it HEADED for interactive login
import httpx, time
port = 9223
tabs = httpx.get(f'http://127.0.0.1:{port}/json/list').json()
if tabs: httpx.get(f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/json/close/{tabs[0]['id']}")   # close one tab by target id
cdp = syncy(cdp_connect(port=port))
try: syncy(cdp.quit())                        # quit browser+connection; raises ConnectionClosedOK as the socket drops
except Exception: pass
time.sleep(1.5)
assert not _debug_running(port), 'browser should be down after quit()'
syncy(cdp_setup(port, headless=False))        # relaunch HEADED so you can log in by hand
assert _debug_running(port)
print('headed Chrome ready on', port, '— log in, then reuse it via fetch(url, session=True)')

headed Chrome ready on 9223 — log in, then reuse it via fetch(url, session=True)



App windows
cdp_app opens a URL in the debug Chrome as an app window, without tabs or an address bar, which suits a local web app. It reuses the running browser when there is one, so all its windows share the same profile and logins. It returns ok, the url, the port, the profile folder, reused (whether a browser was already running) and target, the id of the new window once Chrome reports it. The first test checks the launch flags without starting a browser and the second runs cdp_app against stand-ins for Chrome.

# cdp_app's flags: an app window, headed, on the persistent profile. No browser is launched here.
flags = _chrome_flags(9223, _profile_dir(), False, ['--app=http://alpha.localhost:5001/'])
assert '--app=http://alpha.localhost:5001/' in flags
assert '--headless=new' not in flags                  # an app window you cannot see is useless
assert f'--user-data-dir={_profile_dir()}' in flags   # same profile as cdp_setup, so logins carry
assert str(_profile_dir()).endswith('cdp-chrome')
assert _profile_dir('~/x') == Path.home()/'x'         # user_data_dir wins, and ~ is expanded


# cdp_app end to end against a stubbed browser: reuse a running Chrome, report its target.
# The stubs rebind this notebook's own names, because that is what `cdp_app` resolves at call
# time -- patching `fossick.cdp` would leave the definitions in these cells untouched.
import httpx, subprocess as _sp

_saved = (debug_ready, _sp.Popen, httpx.get)
launched = []
class _Targets:
    def json(self): return [{'id': 'target-1', 'url': 'http://alpha.localhost:5001/'}]
try:
    debug_ready = lambda port, host='127.0.0.1': True     # a debug Chrome is already up
    _sp.Popen = lambda args, **kw: launched.append(args)
    httpx.get = lambda url, **kw: _Targets()
    r = cdp_app('http://alpha.localhost:5001/', wait=1)
finally:
    debug_ready, _sp.Popen, httpx.get = _saved

assert r['ok'] and r['reused'] is True         # reused, so no second resident browser
assert r['target'] == 'target-1'               # and the window was found by its url
assert r['url'] == 'http://alpha.localhost:5001/' and r['port'] == 9223
assert '--app=http://alpha.localhost:5001/' in launched[0]
assert f'--user-data-dir={_profile_dir()}' in launched[0]
print('cdp_app:', {k: r[k] for k in ('reused', 'target')})

cdp_app: {'reused': True, 'target': 'target-1'}



# Open two app windows on one browser and confirm the second reused the first's process.
a = cdp_app('https://example.com/')
b = cdp_app('https://example.org/')
assert a['ok'] and b['ok']
assert b['reused'], 'the second window should reuse the browser the first one started'
assert a['profile'] == b['profile']
print('windows:', a['target'], b['target'], '| reused:', a['reused'], b['reused'])

Recording network requests
calls records the requests a page sends while it loads. Given a url, it opens that page in a new tab and listens until tail seconds after it loads. Without one it only listens, for twice tail seconds. It returns a dictionary keyed by request id, holding each request whose URL matches pattern and, where Chrome still has it, the response body under response_body. replay_xhr in fossick.core can then send any of them again without the browser.

title: cdp
text:
Acting on a page
An agent needs to know what it can click or type into, and a full page of HTML is far too long to read for that. snapshot builds a short text view from the accessibility tree, the description of the page that screen readers use. Each control becomes one line, [#id] role "name", such as [#42] button "Add to cart", where the id is Chrome’s number for that element. With interactive=False it also lists headings, forms and other landmarks.
The other methods act on the page. type_text clears a field before typing, unlike fastcdp’s fill_text, which adds to what is already there. click_settle clicks and then waits for the page to settle, without failing when a click on a single-page app does not navigate. fill_form fills fields by their visible label or name, given as {label: value}, chooses options in drop-downs, optionally clicks a submit button by its name, and returns a fresh snapshot.

Screenshots and annotation
collect gathers screenshots while a person browses. It adds a small bar with a capture button and a done button to the page. Each press of capture saves a screenshot, with the bar hidden. It stops when done is pressed, when count screenshots have been taken, or after tout seconds, and with every_n it also takes one every every_n seconds by itself. Screenshots are saved as PNG files in save_dir when one is given, and returned. BUTTON_JS, HIDE and SHOW are the scripts that draw, hide and show the bar.

title: search
text:
search asks several search engines the same question at once and merges their answers into one list. Asking several engines helps because each one misses pages the others find, and a page that several engines rank highly is usually a good one. The engines are reached through ddgs, which needs no API keys. The lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion, explained below, and can then be reordered by how well each result matches the query.
google gets Google’s own ranking by loading the results page in a stealth browser, which is slower. research goes a step further than either: it searches, downloads the best results that have readable text, and returns them as one markdown digest that cites each source, ready to hand to a language model.

title: search
text:
Asking each engine
For text search, fossick queries each engine in TEXT_BACKENDS separately and keeps each engine’s results in the order that engine ranked them. It does not use ddgs’s own combined search, which picks engines at random and favours Wikipedia. backends lists every engine ddgs offers for a category. With pages above 1, fossick asks each engine for that many pages of results, and drops results on later pages that repeat earlier ones. The test below checks that the ranks keep counting across pages.

    category:str='text'

Return the names of every ddgs engine available for category.

title: search
text:
Merging the lists
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists without needing the engines’ own scores, which are not comparable. Each page gets 1/(k + rank) from every list it appears in, and those amounts are added up. A page ranked first by one engine scores more than a page ranked eighth, and a page found by several engines adds up a score from each. k, 60 by default, controls how much more the top ranks count than the lower ones.
rrf treats two URLs as the same page when they differ only in scheme, www., a trailing slash or tracking parameters, using norm_url from fossick.quality. For each page it keeps the longest snippet any engine gave, the fused score, and engines, the list of engines that found it.


source

rrf
def rrf(
    lists:list, # ranked result lists, one per backend
    k:int=60, # RRF damping constant
)->list:
Merge ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion, scoring each URL by the sum of 1/(k+rank) over the lists it appears in.

title: search
text:
Reranking
Search engines rank by many things besides relevance to the exact words asked. rerank reorders results by how well their title, snippet and URL match the query, and blends that with the merged score. mix is the weight given to the merged score, 0.4 by default; at 1 the reranker is ignored. Each result gains a rerank field holding its relevance score.
method chooses the scorer. 'lexical' uses BM25, a standard word-matching formula, computed with bm25 over the results themselves, so no index is needed. 'flashrank' uses flashrank’s small cross-encoder model, which reads the query and each result together and is better at matching meaning; it needs pip install flashrank, and flashrank_scores returns None when it is missing. 'auto' uses flashrank when installed and BM25 otherwise. 'none', the default for search, keeps the merged order.


source

    mix:float=0.4, # weight on the retrieval score vs the reranker (1 = ignore the reranker)
)->list:
Reorder hits by relevance to q, blending the reranker’s score with the merged search score.

title: search
text:
Where and when
The best answer to many questions depends on the country: building rules, prices and what is for sale all differ. Search engines take a region code of the form country-language, such as au-en. With region='auto', the default, fossick works the two halves out separately from the query.
infer_country looks for country names, adjectives and big cities from COUNTRY_WORDS, and answers only when exactly one country is named; a query comparing two countries gets None. infer_language counts common function words from LANG_WORDS, such as “the” and “what” or “der” and “und”, and answers only when one language clearly leads with at least two matches. infer_region joins them. A query that names no language takes the usual language of the country it names, from COUNTRY_LANG, and whatever the query leaves open comes from the default, us-en. So an English question about France gives fr-en: French sources, in English where possible.
timelimit keeps only recent results: 'd', 'w', 'm' or 'y' for the past day, week, month or year.


source

title: search
text:
research
research turns a question into a set of readable sources. It goes through these steps:

plan, from fossick.quality, splits a question that asks several things into one search per part, and keeps the original question as the first search.
Each search runs with search, or with google when engine='google'. Their results are interleaved, taking one from each in turn, so that each part of the question gets sources.
With curated=True, the default, curate removes sites that copy other sites’ content and moves authoritative sources up. Copycats are dropped before any page is downloaded.
It downloads the candidates in order, n at a time, with fetch(auto=True), until it has n pages with at least 400 characters of readable markdown. A page that failed, was blocked, or was too short goes into dropped with its reason, and the next candidate takes its place.
With focused=True, focus cuts each page down to about chars characters of the passages that best answer the question.

It returns a dictionary with the query, the sources, the digest, the dropped pages, the region it used, the curation report and the plan. Each source holds its title, href, the fetch tier that worked, its publication date, the queries it answered and its markdown in md. The digest joins the sources, separated by ---, each headed by its title, URL, publication date when known, and the part of the question it answers.
Three helpers are useful on their own. page_date finds the date a page says it was published, from its JSON-LD data, its <meta> tags (the names in DATE_META), a <time> element, or a /2018/09/ style URL, and returns it as YYYY-MM-DD, or None. usable checks that a fetched page is a real 200 response, not a bot wall, and has at least min_chars characters of readable markdown; min_chars=0 skips the length check. focus keeps the parts of a long page that answer a query: it keeps the opening blocks up to 30% of the budget, because reference pages often answer in their first paragraphs, then adds the blocks that score best for the query, and returns them in their original order with … marking the gaps.
The cell below this one tests paging with stand-in engines.

# pagination: ranks run on across pages, and page 2's repeats of page 1 don't get counted twice
_seen = []
def _fake(be, q, region='us-en', page=1, timeout=8, tries=2, **kw):
    _seen.append((be, page))
    start = (page-1)*2
    return [dict(title=f'{be}{i}', href=f'https://e.com/{be}/{i}', body='', engine=be, rank=i-start+1)
            for i in range(start, start+3)]        # 3 hits/page, overlapping the next page by one
_real, _engine_hits = _engine_hits, _fake
try:
    one = _backend_lists('q', ('brave',), pages=1)
    two = _backend_lists('q', ('brave',), pages=2)
finally: _engine_hits = _real

assert sorted(_seen) == [('brave',1), ('brave',1), ('brave',2)], _seen   # one job per (backend, page)
assert len(one[0]) == 3 and len(two[0]) == 5                             # 3+3 minus the one repeat
assert [h['rank'] for h in two[0]] == [1,2,3,4,5]                        # continuous, not 1,2,3,1,2,3
assert len({h['href'] for h in two[0]}) == 5                             # deduped within the backend

title: mcp
text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for an AI agent, such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, to discover and call tools that run outside it. This module offers fossick’s functions as MCP tools. The agent sees each tool’s name, arguments and docstring, so the docstrings here are written for the agent and say when to use each option. They are the tools’ interface and are left longer than the docstrings elsewhere in fossick.
The tools take the same arguments as the Python functions they wrap, plus a limit on how much text they return, such as max_chars. Long results are cut at that limit and end with a note saying how many characters were cut, so an agent knows to ask for more. Results are converted to plain JSON types before they are returned. The server talks over standard input and output by default.

title: fossick
text:
fossick gets text off the web and into a program. You give it a search query, a URL, an arXiv id, a YouTube link, a GitHub repository or a local file, and it gives back markdown that a person or a language model can read. It was written for AI agents that need to look things up, so its functions return plain data (strings, lists and dictionaries) that can be printed or passed to a model as they are.
The library works in layers. search sends a query to several search engines at once and merges their answers into one ranked list. read takes a single target and returns its text. Under read, fetch downloads a page and to_md turns its HTML into markdown. Many sites refuse plain downloads from scripts, so fetch can also load a page in a headless browser, in a stealth browser built to pass bot checks, or in a copy of Chrome you have logged in to. For pages that need clicking and typing, cdp_connect drives that Chrome directly. Everything here is also available from the shell as the fossick command and to agents as an MCP server.

title: fossick
text:
One function for every source
read is the function to reach for when you have a target and want its text. It first calls what_is to decide what the target is, and the answer names the reader it will use: dir for a local folder, file for a local file, arxiv for an arXiv URL or id, youtube for a YouTube link, github for a repository, ghfile for a file on GitHub, pdf for a URL ending in .pdf or /pdf, and web for any other http or https URL. A path that exists on disk wins over every URL rule.
Whatever the reader, the result has the same seven fields:







field
holds




ok
True when the reader produced content


kind
the reader used, one of the names above


title
the title, or the first heading of the text


source
the URL, or the absolute path of a local file


text
the content as markdown


skipped
why nothing was read, when ok is False


meta
details from that reader, such as the authors of a paper or the HTTP status of a page, and the time it was read



Here read opens this repository’s own README:

target = str(repo_root()/'README.md')
assert what_is(target) == 'file'
result = read(target)
assert sorted(result) == ['kind', 'meta', 'ok', 'skipped', 'source', 'text', 'title']
assert (result.ok, result.kind, result.title) == (True, 'file', 'fossick')
assert '# fossick' in result.text and result.skipped is None
result.kind, result.title, result.ok

A folder or a GitHub repository is a tree of files rather than one document, so read does not turn it into text. It returns ok=True with an empty text and puts the local path in meta['path'], and the caller decides which files to open. For a GitHub repository that path is a fresh clone in fossick’s cache. With pages=True, a PDF comes back as a list of (page_index, text) pairs, counted from 0, so that a citation can point at a page.
Sometimes a target is recognised but yields nothing: a site serves a bot check instead of the page, a YouTube video has no English captions, or a URL that looked like a PDF returns something else. read reports these with ok=False and a reason in skipped, and does not raise. It raises ValueError only when the target is none of the kinds above.

A logged-in Chrome
Some pages are only shown to a logged-in user. fossick reaches them through a separate copy of Chrome that runs with remote debugging switched on, on port 9223, with its own profile in ~/.cache/fastcdp/cdp-chrome. cdp_connect starts it the first time it is needed. text:
Downloading pages

Refusing private addresses
A program that fetches URLs chosen by an AI agent can be tricked into fetching addresses inside your own network, such as a router’s admin page or a cloud server’s metadata service, which hands out credentials. This is called server-side request forgery. check_url refuses any URL that is not http or https, any host name such as localhost or metadata.google.internal, and any host that resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or other non-public address. It raises BlockedURL, whose message names the two ways round it: pass allow_private=True to one call, or set the environment variable FOSSICK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1 for the whole process. Every download in fossick goes through get_page, which runs this check first.

get_page is the single function every download passes through. It runs check_url, then downloads the page in one of four ways. By default it sends a plain HTTP request. heavy=True loads the page in a headless browser so that its JavaScript runs. stealthy=True uses scrapling’s stealth browser, which is built to pass bot checks such as Cloudflare’s. session=True uses the logged-in Chrome described in fossick.cdp, with its cookies. The browsers are imported only when first needed, and if they cannot be loaded get_page raises BrowserUnavailable instead of quietly returning nothing.
http_get and http_post are get_page with the method set and a 30 second timeout. http_page sends a plain request with any of GET, POST, PUT or DELETE and skips the address check, so use it only for URLs your own code chose. Most callers want fetch, below, rather than any of these.


source

get_page

    url, method:str='GET', payload:NoneType=None, heavy:bool=False, stealthy:bool=False, session:bool=False,
    allow_private:NoneType=None, **kw
)->scrapling.engines.toolbelt.custom.Response:
Download url with plain HTTP, a headless browser, the stealth browser or the logged-in debug Chrome, after checking it with check_url.

    url, method:str='GET', payload:NoneType=None, verify:bool=False, **kw
)->scrapling.engines.toolbelt.custom.Response:
Send one plain HTTP request with scrapling’s Fetcher and return the response, without the private address check.




source

BrowserUnavailable
def BrowserUnavailable(
    *args, **kwargs
):
The error raised when scrapling’s browser fetchers fail to import; the message suggests running scrapling install.



r1=get_page('https://httpbin.org/get', verify=False)
r1.__dict__.keys()


from fastcore.test import test_fail


try: get_page('https://httpbin.org/put', method='PUT', verify=False)
except AssertionError as e: test_fail(str(e) == 'Only GET and POST methods are supported')


http_page('https://httpbin.org/put', method='PUT', verify=False).status



fetch
fetch is the function most code should call to download a page. It wraps get_page and returns scrapling’s response object with two attributes added: html, holding the page or only the part matching sel, and xhr, holding the background requests recorded when capture_xhr=True. The response also has status, url, and a json() method for JSON replies.
Choosing the right download method by hand is guesswork, so auto=True tries them in turn: plain HTTP, then the headless browser, then the stealth browser, then the stealth browser through the logged-in Chrome. It stops at the first response that is not a bot wall and records the method that worked in tier, or 'blocked' if none did. Each failed attempt and its reason is kept in errs.
browser_session is for downloading many pages with a browser. Starting a browser takes seconds, so instead of one per URL it opens one for the length of a with block and gives you a fetch-like function that reuses it.


source

browser_session
def browser_session(
    stealthy:bool=False, headless:bool=True, **init_kw
):
Keep one browser open for a with block and yield a fetch(url, sel=None) function that reuses it.




source

fetch
def fetch(
    url:str, # URL to fetch
    sel:str=None, # CSS selector to extract (None = full page)
    method:str='GET', # HTTP method; 'POST' sends payload as JSON body
    payload:dict=None, # POST body (JSON) or GET query params
    heavy:bool=False, # Full JS rendering via headless browser
    stealthy:bool=False, # Anti-bot stealth fetcher (Cloudflare etc.)
    capture_xhr:bool=False, # Capture XHR calls made by the page (only works with heavy or stealthy)
    session:bool=False, # Route through the persistent debug Chrome (reuses its logged-in cookies); True or a port int
    auto:bool=False, # Try plain, heavy, stealthy, then the debug Chrome, stopping at the first response that is not a bot wall
    allow_private:bool=None, # Allow localhost/intranet targets (default: refuse; $FOSSICK_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1)
    **kw
)->scrapling.engines.toolbelt.custom.Response: # Extra kwargs passed to scrapling (e.g. verify, headers)
Download url and return the response with .html set to the page, or the part matching sel, and .xhr set to any recorded background requests.




Bot walls
Many sites put a challenge page in front of their content for visitors they think are scripts. Cloudflare’s “Just a moment” page and the Anubis proof-of-work page are common examples. The challenge often arrives with status 200, so it looks like a successful download. fossick treats a response as blocked when its status is 401, 403, 429, 503 or 530, when its HTML contains the marker of a known challenge or captcha widget, or when it is a 200 response with less than 200 characters of HTML. The tests below check these rules, including that a page which only mentions the word captcha is not counted as blocked.
The cells after that run against real sites and are not run by the tests. They show a Cloudflare and an Anubis wall being detected, auto=True stopping at the plain tier for a page that needs nothing more, browser_session reusing one browser for two pages, and session=True going through the logged-in Chrome.

# A site behind Cloudflare: a plain fetch hits the bot wall, and _blocked() flags it for escalation
cf = fetch('https://www.scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge', verify=False)
assert cf.status == 403, f'expected a Cloudflare 403 challenge, got {cf.status}'
assert _blocked(cf) is True            # fetch(auto=True) escalates from here (heavy -> stealthy -> session)
print('cloudflare:', cf.status, '| blocked?', _blocked(cf))


# A site behind Anubis (proof-of-work bot wall): _blocked() now recognizes it, so fetch(auto=True) escalates
an = fetch('https://anubis.techaro.lol/', verify=False)
assert 'making sure' in an.html.lower(), 'expected the Anubis challenge page'
assert _blocked(an) is True            # Anubis markers are in _BLOCK_MARKERS -> auto escalates past this wall
print('anubis wall detected by _blocked?', _blocked(an))


# regression: a normal page that merely *mentions* captcha must NOT read as a bot wall.
# Wikipedia embeds hCaptcha config keys in its page JS -- the word is there, but there's no challenge widget.
wiki = fetch('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anubis', verify=False)
assert wiki.status == 200 and 'captcha' in wiki.html.lower()   # the word IS present on the page...
assert _blocked(wiki) is False   # ...but _BLOCK_MARKERS matches captcha *widgets* (g-recaptcha/h-captcha/...), not the word


# fetch(auto=True): walks plain->heavy->stealthy->session, stops at the first unblocked tier, tags .tier
plain = fetch('https://example.com', auto=True, verify=False)
assert plain.status == 200 and plain.tier == 'plain'   # a static page needs no escalation
print('example.com ->', plain.tier)


# browser_session(): open ONE browser, reuse it across fetches (skips per-URL relaunch)
with browser_session() as bf:
    a = bf('https://example.com')
    b = bf('https://httpbin.org/html')
assert a.status == 200 and b.status == 200
assert len(a.html) > 0 and len(b.html) > 0


# fetch(session=True): route through the persistent debug Chrome, reusing its logged-in cookies
pg = fetch('https://httpbin.org/headers', session=True)
assert pg.status == 200
print(pg.html[:200])

Crawling and batches
crawl visits pages breadth-first, starting from one URL and following the links that match follow_sel, until it has visited max_pages pages. By default it stays on the starting site. It returns the responses that came back with status 200, and a page that fails to download is reported and skipped. delay waits between requests so as not to load a small site heavily. For crawls with heavy or stealthy, one browser is kept open for the whole crawl unless reuse=False.

text:
PDFs and arXiv papers
get_pdf downloads a PDF, or reads one from disk, and returns it as a PdfDocument from pdf_oxide, or None when the bytes are not a PDF. It decides by looking for the %PDF- signature at the start of the file, not at the URL, because arXiv serves papers from URLs with no .pdf ending. It also passes the small proof-of-work check that the NCBI PubMed Central archive puts in front of its PDFs. With save_path set to a folder or a file name, it keeps a copy of the file. The examples download two papers from the Self-Determination Theory site and print the start of their text.


source

    url_or_path:str, # URL or local path to PDF
    save_path:NoneType=None, # optional path to save the PDF (directory or full path)
    **scrapling_kw
)->pdf_oxide.pdf_oxide.PdfDocument | None: # extra kwargs passed to scrapling fetcher (e.g. verify, headers, timeout)
Download a PDF from a URL, or read one from disk, and return it as a PdfDocument, or None when the bytes are not a PDF.



import tempfile


sp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())


sdt = 'https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2000_RyanDeci_SDT.pdf'
sdt_p = get_pdf(sdt, save_path=sp, verify=False)


sdt_p.to_markdown_all()[:200]


gdr = 'https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/1997_GrolnickDeciRyan.pdf'
gcr = get_pdf(gdr, save_path=sp, verify=False)


gcr.to_markdown_all()[:200]

_c = _md2cells('# Intro\n\nSome prose.\n\n[code]\n\n> 1+1\n2\n[/code]\n\n## Next\n\nMore.')
assert [(c.cell_type, c.source) for c in _c] == [('markdown','# Intro\n\nSome prose.'), ('code','1+1\n# => 2'), ('markdown','## Next\n\nMore.')], _c

finally: fetch = _rf

try: _pp = pdf2nb(str(_t/'a.pdf'), nb_path=_t/'attn.ipynb', ocr_selection='off')
finally: pdf_md = _rp

GitHub
gh_clone returns a local copy of a repository. The first call clones it into fossick’s cache folder, over HTTPS first and then SSH, so a private repository works if you have an SSH key. Later calls fetch and reset the clone to the latest commit. Git runs with /dev/null as stdin, so it never reads the caller’s terminal. title: core
section: Finding the API behind a page
text:
Finding the API behind a page
Many modern pages arrive nearly empty and then load their data with background requests from JavaScript, called XHR or fetch calls, which usually return JSON. Reading that JSON directly is faster and more reliable than scraping the rendered page. find_xhr loads a page in a headless browser, records the background requests it makes, and returns each one whose URL matches pattern as a dictionary with url, content_type and the decoded data. With session=True it records the requests through the logged-in Chrome instead, and each result also carries a capture. replay_xhr sends a captured request again as a plain HTTP call with the browser’s cookies, which is how you call an API that needs you to be logged in without keeping a browser open.
pattern can be a regular expression, such as .*products.*, or a shell-style glob, such as *products*. compile_pattern accepts both: it tries the text as a regular expression and, when that is invalid, reads it as a glob.


source

replay_xhr
def replay_xhr(
    capture:dict, # a request dict from cdp.calls() or find_xhr(session=True)[i].capture
    data:NoneType=None, # override request body (str/dict); defaults to the captured body
    port:int=9223, # debug Chrome port to pull cookies from
    use_cookies:bool=True, # attach the browser's cookies for this domain (keeps auth)
    **kw
)->scrapling.engines.toolbelt.custom.Response: # Extra kwargs passed to the underlying Fetcher (headers, params, verify)
Send a request captured from the browser again as a plain HTTP call, with the debug Chrome’s cookies for that site.




source

find_xhr
def find_xhr(
    url:str, # URL to visit with browser
    pattern:str='*', # Glob or regex pattern to filter captured XHR URLs
    session:bool=False, # Use the persistent debug Chrome (authenticated) instead of a throwaway browser
    port:int=9223, # debug Chrome port (only when session=True)
    tail:int=3, # seconds to keep listening after navigation (only when session=True)
    **kw
)->list: # Extra kwargs passed to fetch (verify, network_idle, etc.)
Load url in a browser and return the background requests it makes whose URLs match pattern.




source

compile_pattern
def compile_pattern(
    pattern
):
Compile pattern as a regular expression, or as a shell-style glob such as *foo* when it is not a valid one.



assert compile_pattern('.*products.*').search('https://api.example.com/products?q=1')
assert compile_pattern('*products*').search('https://api.example.com/products?q=1')
assert not compile_pattern('*products*').search('https://api.example.com/search')
assert compile_pattern('.*[Ss]earch.*').search('https://api.example.com/Search')

An API rarely returns its records at the top level of the JSON. They might be under results, or several levels down at data.products.items. json_records finds them by searching the whole payload for the longest list of dictionaries, and with_key=True also tells you which key held it.
paginate_api reads every page of a paged JSON API. It sends the request repeatedly, raising the page number in page_field each time, and stops when a page comes back empty or shorter than the page size, or after max_pages pages. It finds each page’s records with results_field if you name one and json_records if you do not. With save=True each page is written to a file, and a later run reads the saved pages instead of fetching them again.

    results_field:str=None, # Response key with items list (auto-detect if None)
    method:str='POST', # HTTP method

    page_start:int=1, # Starting page number (default 1)
    save:bool=False, # If True, saves each page's items to disk
    save_file:str='{url}_page_{page}.json', # Filepath pattern for saving (only used if save=True)
    force:bool=False, # If True, forces re-fetching even if saved file exists
    **kw
)->list: # Extra kwargs passed to fetch() (verify, headers, etc.)
Request successive pages of a JSON API and return the items from every page in one list.

Return the longest list of dictionaries found anywhere in a decoded JSON payload.


download_files saves every file linked from a page whose link matches pattern, for example *.pdf or .*\.ipynb$. With follow=True it first crawls from the page, so it can collect files spread over a series of pages. Files already on disk are not downloaded again unless force=True. The example walks the JAX tutorial pages by their “next” links and saves each notebook.

    heavy:bool=False, stealthy:bool=False, **kw
)->list[pathlib.Path]: # Extra kwargs passed to fetch/http_get (e.g. verify)
Download every file linked from url whose link matches pattern, optionally crawling linked pages first, and return the saved paths.



jax, fs = 'https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/notebooks/thinking_in_jax.html', 'a[class="right-next"]'
download_files(jax, follow=True, follow_sel=fs, file_sel='a[href$=".ipynb"]', save_dir=sp, verify=False)


from fastcore.test import test_eq


_pages = crawl('https://lego.sankalpa.sh/', max_pages=2, verify=False)
assert isinstance(_pages, list), f"Expected list, got {type(_pages)}"
assert len(_pages) > 0, "Expected at least one page"
assert all(p.status == 200 for p in _pages), "Non-200 pages should be skipped"
assert all(len(p.html) > 0 for p in _pages), "html should be non-empty"
assert len({p.url for p in _pages}) == len(_pages), "url values should be unique"


# crawl(reuse=True): a JS-rendered crawl keeps ONE browser open across pages (no per-page relaunch)
_jsp = crawl('https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/', max_pages=2, heavy=True, reuse=True)
assert _jsp and all(p.status == 200 for p in _jsp)
assert all(len(p.html) > 500 for p in _jsp)      # JS actually rendered content into the DOM


# Step 1: visit the listing page with a headless browser, capture all XHR/fetch calls
apis = find_xhr('https://www.danmurphys.com.au/list/wine-all', verify=False)


# paginate_api: test with JSONPlaceholder (free public REST API, GET-based)
posts = paginate_api(
    'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts',
    payload={'_page': 1, '_limit': 5},
    page_field='_page',
    size_field='_limit',
    method='GET',
    verify=False,
)
assert len(posts) >= 5
assert 'title' in posts[0]

find_xhr(session=True) records requests through the logged-in Chrome, so a request that needs your cookies can be captured and then replayed with replay_xhr:

# find_xhr(session=True) -> replay_xhr: capture a request via the authenticated debug Chrome,
# then replay it as a fast plain-HTTP call using the browser's cookies
hits = find_xhr('https://httpbin.org/json', pattern='.*json', session=True)
assert hits, 'no matching request captured'
assert hits[0].capture, 'each hit should carry a replayable capture'
r = replay_xhr(hits[0].capture)
assert r.status == 200
print(hits[0].url, '->', r.status)

title: core
text:
YouTube
These three functions use yt-dlp. search_yt searches YouTube and returns a list of result dictionaries. read_yt returns one video’s details and its transcript, built from YouTube’s English automatic captions, under the key source; a video without them gets an empty transcript. Results are cached on disk by video id. download_yt saves a video’s audio as mp3, which needs ffmpeg installed, or its video as mp4. All three accept verify=False to skip certificate checks, which helps behind a proxy that rewrites HTTPS.


source

text:
Checkout forms
shop_fields lists every visible form field on the page with its number, label, autocomplete token, current value and, for drop-downs, the options. It is the reliable source for filling a form, because nothing has to be guessed from the field names. Password values are never returned.
shop_fill fills a form from a profile dictionary with standard keys: first_name, last_name, email, phone, address1, address2, city, state, postcode, country, company, notes and the card_* keys. match_fields decides which field each key goes into. It trusts the field’s autocomplete token first, then its name or id, then its label, using the words in FIELD_MAP, which include Australian wording such as “suburb” and “postcode”. Each field is used for one key at most. A numeric key, such as '7', fills field number 7 from shop_fields directly, for choices like size or delivery time that have no standard key. After filling, the form is read again to confirm what each field now holds. shop_set sets one field by its number.
shop_fill(submit=...) clicks a button by its name afterwards. A button whose name matches PAY_RX, such as “Pay now” or “Place order”, is clicked only when confirm=True is also passed; without it shop_fill raises ShopError and fills nothing.

Tests
The offline tests cover the site hints, matching profile keys to a realistic checkout form, the rule for when a cart has changed, choosing a product by number or title, the payment button guard, and cart line lookup. assert site_hint('https://www.coles.com.au/search/products?q=milk')['cart'].endswith('/trolley')
assert site_hint('https://www.amazon.com.au/s?k=x')['search'] == 'https://www.amazon.com.au/s?k={q}'

assert site_hint('https://some-random-shopify-store.com') == {}     # generic path, no hints needed


#: a checkout form in the shape real ones come in: AU wording, mixed autocomplete coverage, decoys

    dict(i=1, tag='input', type='email', name='customer[email]', id='e', autocomplete='email', label='Email address', options=None),

    dict(i=4, tag='input', type='tel', name='contact', id='', autocomplete='tel', label='Email or phone', options=None),
    dict(i=5, tag='input', type='text', name='address1', id='', autocomplete=None, label='Address', options=None),

    dict(i=9, tag='input', type='text', name='zip', id='', autocomplete='postal-code', label='Postcode', options=None),

Limits
fossick does not solve captchas, and it never clicks a payment button unless the call passes confirm=True. Stores change their pages over time and the in-page script may stop finding a store’s controls, which is why every action checks the cart and reports what it saw rather than assuming the click worked.

title: quality
text:
A search engine ranks pages by how well they match a query, which is not the same as how worth reading they are. A question about building rules in Australia can come back with five cost guides from one trade directory ahead of the government page that sets the rules, and a programming question can come back with sites that copy Stack Overflow answers. This module fixes that before any page is downloaded. It removes copycat sites, moves sources with authority on the kind of question asked up the list, and stops one website from filling the whole list. It also splits a question that asks several things into one search per part.
research in fossick.search uses all of this when curated=True, its default. Each function here also works on its own, on any list of result dictionaries with an href or url.

title: quality
section: Which site a URL belongs to
text:
Which site a URL belongs to
Two URLs belong to the same site when they share a registrable domain, the part of the name someone registered: docs.python.org and www.python.org both belong to python.org. Usually that is the last two parts of the host name. In countries whose registries sell names one level down, such as bbc.co.uk or nsw.gov.au, it is the last three. MULTI_LABEL_SUFFIXES lists those registry endings for the countries fossick handles. host returns a URL’s host name in lower case without www., and registrable_domain returns the site.

The same page often appears under several URLs: with and without www., with a trailing slash, or with tracking parameters such as utm_source added by whoever shared it. norm_url reduces a URL to one key by dropping the scheme, the www., the fragment, tracking parameters, a default port and a trailing slash, and by sorting the query parameters. title: quality
text:
Authority depends on the question
Which sources deserve trust depends on what is asked. For a question about the law, a government site is the authority; for a question about a library, its documentation is; for a question about what users think, a forum is. DOMAIN_RULES lists, for each kind of question (docs, policy, release, security and community), the sites to move up and the sites to move down.
A rule can take three forms, and domain_matches checks them. A rule ending in a dot, such as docs., matches host names that start with it. A rule starting with a dot, such as .gov.au, matches every host under that ending and the ending itself. Any other rule, such as sec.gov, matches that domain and its subdomains. A rule never matches just because a host name starts with it, so openai.com.evil.example does not count as openai.com. blocked_matches applies the same exact-or-subdomain test to a blocked list.

What kind of question it is
classify reads the kind of question from cue words in INTENT_CUES: “regulation” and “permit” suggest policy, “release notes” suggests release, and so on. It returns the kind with the most cues, and None when there are no cues or two kinds tie. None means the results are not reordered by authority, which is safer than reordering them by a wrong guess.

Copycat sites and site:
SPAM_MIRRORS lists sites that copy other sites’ content, such as Stack Overflow scrapers and GitHub mirrors. They add nothing over the original, and searching several engines tends to promote them, because they are built to rank on all of them. drop_spam removes them, along with any extra domains in blocked, and returns the remaining results and the domains removed. allowed keeps a domain that would otherwise be removed.
A query containing site:reddit.com has already chosen its site. site_domains reads those choices, and curate then skips both the copycat removal and the one-site limit, which would otherwise undo the choice.

title: quality
text:
Splitting a question into searches
A question such as “I want to rebuild my garage in australia, cheap options, what is the regulation on it, material options” asks three things, and one search for all of it mostly finds pages about the first. plan splits it into one search per part. It removes openings such as “I want to” (LEAD_INS) and empty phrases (FILLER), splits the rest at commas, question marks and words such as “and”, and adds the subject of the first part to each later part, so each search still says “garage australia”. The original question is always the first search.
plan returns just [q] when there is nothing to split: a query shorter than min_words words, a query with site:, or a query whose parts add nothing to the first. max_queries caps the number of searches. Pass rewrite, a function such as a call to a language model that returns a list of searches, to use it instead of these rules. facets returns the parts as lists of topic words.
interleave merges the result lists of several searches by taking one from each in turn, and keeps a page that several searches found only once, recording every search that found it in queries. Taking turns gives each part of the question its own sources. Merging by score would favour the general guide that ranks for every part over the specific source that answers one.

section: How many stories, not how many URLs
text:
How many stories, not how many URLs
Ten results can be one story: a news agency report reprinted by nine sites. cluster_sources groups results that are the same page, by norm_url, or that share most of their text. Text is compared by jaccard similarity over shingles, the sets of three-word sequences in each result’s title and text: the size of the overlap divided by the size of the union. Two results at or above threshold, 0.6 by default, are one story, and the grouping carries through, so if A matches B and B matches C, all three are one group. Each group is named after its first member in the input order.
independence summarises the groups as a score that rises with the number of separate stories and of separate sites, and states its limits: two sites that rewrite one press release in their own words do not share enough text to be grouped.

Describing a result list
diversity describes a list without changing it: how many results and sites it holds, the dominant_domain and the share of results it holds, how many URLs repeat, how many pairs of results read alike (near_dups), and how many separate stories there are (sources). score combines the share of separate sites, unique URLs and unlike pairs into one number between 0 and 1, higher for a more varied list. snippet_similarity compares two pieces of text by their three-word sequences.

text:
Tests
The cells below test each function offline, mostly on the garage question, which is the case this module was written for.

# registrable domain: the site behind a url, with the three-label registries handled
assert registrable_domain('https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html') == 'python.org'
assert registrable_domain('https://www.bbc.co.uk/news') == 'bbc.co.uk'
assert registrable_domain('https://planning.nsw.gov.au/x') == 'nsw.gov.au'
assert registrable_domain('https://wko.at/') == 'wko.at'
assert registrable_domain('https://x.com') == 'x.com' and registrable_domain('') == ''
assert registrable_domain('http://192.168.1.1/a') == '192.168.1.1'      # an ip has nothing to strip
assert host('https://WWW.Example.COM./p') == 'example.com'


# norm_url: one page, one key -- and query order is not identity
assert norm_url('https://www.x.com/a/?utm_source=t#frag') == norm_url('http://x.com/a')
assert norm_url('https://x.com/a') != norm_url('https://x.com/b')
assert norm_url('https://x.com/a?b=2&a=1') == norm_url('https://x.com/a?a=1&b=2')   # sorted
assert norm_url('https://x.com:443/a') == norm_url('https://x.com/a')               # default port
assert norm_url('https://x.com:8443/a') != norm_url('https://x.com/a')              # but not any port
assert norm_url('https://x.com/a?mkt_tok=z&_ga=1&keep=2') == norm_url('https://x.com/a?keep=2')


# rule matching is the security boundary, not just the ranking one
assert domain_matches('docs.python.org', 'docs.') and not domain_matches('notdocs.com', 'docs.')
assert domain_matches('planning.nsw.gov.au', '.gov.au')          # suffix rules cover a whole registry
assert domain_matches('gov.uk', '.gov.uk')                       # ...including the registry itself
assert domain_matches('abcb.gov.au', '.gov.au')
assert not domain_matches('hipages.com.au', '.gov.au')
assert domain_matches('sec.gov', 'sec.gov') and domain_matches('www.sec.gov', 'sec.gov')
assert not domain_matches('openai.com.evil.example', 'openai.com')   # never a bare startswith
assert blocked_matches('de.newbedev.com', 'newbedev.com')
assert not blocked_matches('newbedev.com.evil.example', 'newbedev.com')


# intent: read it off the query, and abstain rather than guess
assert classify('rebuild my garage in australia, what is the regulation on it') == 'policy'
assert classify('planning permission for a garage') == 'policy'
assert classify('latest Tailscale release notes') == 'release'
assert classify('python asyncio api reference') == 'docs'
assert classify('CVE-2024-1234 advisory') is None or classify('log4j vulnerability advisory') == 'security'
assert classify('what do people on reddit think of it') == 'community'
assert classify('best turntables under 1000 euro') is None          # says nothing -> no reranking
assert classify('reddit release notes') is None                     # says two things -> no reranking
assert classify('') is None and classify(None) is None


# spam mirrors are removed; an explicit site: constraint switches the whole thing off
_h = [dict(href='https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1', title='real'),
      dict(href='https://newbedev.com/questions/1', title='mirror'),
      dict(href='https://de.newbedev.com/q/1', title='mirror subdomain')]
_kept, _rm = drop_spam(_h)
assert [h['title'] for h in _kept] == ['real'] and _rm == ['de.newbedev.com', 'newbedev.com']
assert drop_spam(_h, allowed=['newbedev.com'])[0] == _h            # allow rescues the subdomain too

assert site_domains('site:reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA best server') == ['reddit.com']
assert site_domains('plain query', include=['NSW.gov.au']) == ['nsw.gov.au']
_, _r = curate('site:reddit.com best local llm', [dict(href=f'https://reddit.com/{i}') for i in range(5)])
assert _r['site_constrained'] == ['reddit.com'] and _r['demoted'] == 0   # not diversified away


# authority: the garage query, which is what this is all for
_garage = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/article/garage-cost', title='How much to build a garage'),
           dict(href='https://oneflare.com.au/costs/garage', title='Garage costs 2026'),
           dict(href='https://www.planning.nsw.gov.au/exempt-development', title='Exempt development'),
           dict(href='https://airtasker.com/garage', title='Get quotes'),
           dict(href='https://abcb.gov.au/ncc', title='National Construction Code')]
_out, _rep = curate('rebuild my garage in australia, what is the regulation on it', _garage)
assert _rep['intent'] == 'policy'
assert [host(_url(h)) for h in _out][:2] == ['planning.nsw.gov.au', 'abcb.gov.au'], [_url(h) for h in _out]
assert _rep['authority']['applied'] and _rep['authority']['top_before'] == 'hipages.com.au'

# nothing is dropped by reranking -- a lead-gen page is still a price signal, just not the answer
assert len(_out) == len(_garage)

# an unknown or absent intent is a no-op, not an error
assert authority_rerank(_garage, None)[0] == _garage
assert authority_rerank(_garage, 'nonsense')[1]['applied'] is False


# capping and diversity describe the five-listicles-from-one-site failure
_mono = [dict(href=f'https://hipages.com.au/a/{i}', title='Garage cost guide', body='what a garage costs')
         for i in range(5)] + [dict(href='https://abcb.gov.au/ncc', title='NCC', body='construction code')]
_capped, _n = cap_per_domain(_mono, 2)
assert _n == 3 and [host(_url(h)) for h in _capped][:3] == ['hipages.com.au']*2 + ['abcb.gov.au']
assert len(_capped) == len(_mono)                                    # moved, never dropped

_d = diversity(_mono)
assert _d['n'] == 6 and _d['domains'] == 2
assert _d['dominant_domain'] == dict(domain='hipages.com.au', share=round(5/6, 4))
assert _d['near_dups'] > 0                                           # the five guides read alike
assert diversity([])['n'] == 0 and diversity([])['score'] == 0.0

# a genuinely diverse set scores higher than a monopolised one
_div = [dict(href=f'https://s{i}.com/a', title=f'topic {i}', body=f'quite different text number {i}')
        for i in range(6)]
assert diversity(_div)['score'] > _d['score']
assert snippet_similarity('one two three four', 'one two three four') == 1.0
assert snippet_similarity('too short', 'too short') == 0.0           # no trigram evidence -> not a match


# curate is safe on the boring paths
assert curate('anything', [])[0] == []
_h2 = [dict(href='https://a.com/1', title='t')]
assert curate('q', _h2, rerank=False)[0] is _h2                      # describe-only changes nothing
assert 'diversity' in curate('q', _h2, rerank=False)[1]
assert curate('q', _h2, intent=None)[1]['intent'] is None


# planning: one question containing three
_GARAGE = ('I want to rebuild my garage in australia, cheap options, '
           'what is the regulation on it, material options')
_p = plan(_GARAGE)
assert _p[0] == _GARAGE                                   # the baseline is never given up
assert len(_p) == 4                                       # all three facets, plus the original
assert any('regulation' in s for s in _p[1:]), _p
assert any('cheap' in s for s in _p[1:]) and any('material' in s for s in _p[1:]), _p
assert all('garage' in s and 'australia' in s for s in _p[1:]), _p   # subject re-attached to each facet
assert 'want' not in _p[1] and 'what' not in _p[1]        # lead-in and filler stripped

# ...and constant abstention, which is what makes it safe to leave on
assert plan('sqlite wal mode vs journal mode performance') == ['sqlite wal mode vs journal mode performance']
assert plan('garage cost') == ['garage cost']                        # too short to hold two questions
assert plan('site:reddit.com best local llm, cheap options') == ['site:reddit.com best local llm, cheap options']
assert plan(_GARAGE, max_queries=1) == [_GARAGE]                     # explicitly disabled
assert plan('') == []
assert len(plan(_GARAGE, max_queries=2)) == 2                        # the cap is honoured

# a facet that adds no words to the subject is not a search
assert plan('rebuild my garage in australia, the garage, australia') == \
       ['rebuild my garage in australia, the garage, australia']

# an injected rewriter (a model, in ramabana) replaces the heuristic and still keeps the original
assert plan('anything at all here', rewrite=lambda q: ['one', 'two']) == ['anything at all here', 'one', 'two']


# interleaving is coverage, not consensus: the generalist that ranks for every facet must not
# outrank the specialist that owns one
_cost = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/guide', title='complete garage guide'),
         dict(href='https://oneflare.com.au/cost', title='costs')]
_reg  = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/guide', title='complete garage guide'),
         dict(href='https://planning.nsw.gov.au/exempt', title='exempt development')]
_mat  = [dict(href='https://hipages.com.au/guide', title='complete garage guide'),
         dict(href='https://bunnings.com.au/materials', title='materials')]
_il = interleave([_cost, _reg, _mat])
assert [host(_url(h)) for h in _il][:2] == ['hipages.com.au', 'oneflare.com.au']
assert 'planning.nsw.gov.au' in [host(_url(h)) for h in _il[:4]], [_url(h) for h in _il]
assert len(_il) == 4                                      # the guide appears once, not three times

# ragged lists and empties are fine
assert interleave([]) == [] and interleave([[], []]) == []
assert len(interleave([_cost, []])) == 2


# clustering: four urls, one story -- and transitivity is what makes that visible
_wire = ('OpenAI said today that it is lowering prices for its newest model across all tiers, '
         'effective immediately for every API customer.')
_syn = [dict(href='https://a.invalid/x', title='OpenAI cuts prices', body=_wire),
        dict(href='https://b.invalid/y', title='OpenAI cuts prices', body=_wire),
        dict(href='https://c.invalid/z', title='OpenAI cuts prices', body=_wire),
        dict(href='https://openai.com/index/new-pricing', title='New pricing for our latest model',
             body='We are updating the per-token price of our newest model from today.')]
_cl = cluster_sources(_syn)
assert len(_cl) == 2, _cl                                  # three copies collapse, the original stands
assert _cl[0]['size'] == 3 and _cl[1]['size'] == 1
assert _cl[0]['canonical'] == 'https://a.invalid/x'        # named by its first (highest-ranked) member

_ind = independence(_syn)
assert _ind['n'] == 4 and _ind['sources'] == 2             # the number a reader actually needs
assert _ind['method'] == 'url+text' and _ind['confidence'] == 'medium'
assert _ind['limitations']                                 # always says what it cannot see

# transitivity: A~B and B~C is one family even where A and C alone fall short of the threshold
_chain = [dict(href='https://a.invalid/1', body='alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta'),
          dict(href='https://b.invalid/2', body='beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota'),
          dict(href='https://c.invalid/3', body='gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota kappa')]
assert jaccard(shingles(_chain[0]['body']), shingles(_chain[2]['body'])) < 0.6      # not a pair...
assert len(cluster_sources(_chain, threshold=0.5)) == 1, cluster_sources(_chain, 0.5)  # ...but one chain

# the same url twice is one source however differently it is described
assert len(cluster_sources([dict(href='https://x.com/a?utm_source=t', body='one two three four'),
                            dict(href='http://www.x.com/a', body='utterly different words here')])) == 1

# genuinely independent results stay independent
_div = [dict(href=f'https://s{i}.invalid/a', body=f'entirely separate subject number {i} here')
        for i in range(5)]
assert independence(_div)['sources'] == 5 and independence(_div)['score'] > independence(_syn)['score']

# no text to compare: degrade to url identity and say so rather than claiming confidence
_bare = [dict(href='https://a.invalid/1'), dict(href='https://b.invalid/2')]
assert independence(_bare)['method'] == 'url' and independence(_bare)['confidence'] == 'low'
assert any('too little text' in l for l in independence(_bare)['limitations'])
assert independence([]) == dict(n=0, sources=0, score=0.0, clusters=[], method='none',
                                confidence='low', limitations=[])

# and diversity carries the honest source count next to the url count
assert diversity(_syn)['n'] == 4 and diversity(_syn)['sources'] == 2
assert shingles('two words') == set() and jaccard(set(), {('a','b','c')}) == 0.0
